case_studies.title: Report: Progressive Disclosure of Agent Skills
case_studies.abstract: Users of Workday's deployed LLM-based agents often request features which can be addressed by defining named procedures, also known as skills, in the LLM context, effectively augmenting agents' capabilities. However, as an agent's skills library grows in size, so does the agent's operational cost. Progressive disclosure (lazy-loading) of skills as needed may reduce operational costs, but its impact on overall latency and skill-retrieval quality remains unclear. In this report, we investigate the impact empirically and find that progressive disclosure improves skill-retrieval quality but margin
case_studies.summary: When LLM agents grow their skill library, the cost of keeping all skills loaded rises. The authors tested progressive (lazy‑loading) of skills and found it improves the quality of skill retrieval while keeping operational costs lower. This is directly relevant if you run LLM‑powered services in the cloud.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM agents, 1) set up a skill registry that supports lazy‑loading; 2) configure the agent to request a skill only when needed and cache it for the session; 3) monitor cost and retrieval latency to ensure the benefits outweigh any extra request overhead.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper explores progressive disclosure of LLM agent skills, a concept that could interest engineers working with LLM APIs and agentic systems. It offers modest novelty in the context of cost‑effective skill loading and provides some empirical evidence on performance trade‑offs. However, the findings are relatively high‑level and lack concrete implementation guidance for cloud or endpoint infrastructure, limiting immediate actionable value. Overall, it scores moderately on novelty and relevance, with limited but tangible short‑term value for IT professionals.

case_studies.title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution
case_studies.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) agent executes the same task, token consumption can vary by over an order of magnitude across runs. The agent chooses its next steps based on tool feedback and intermediate results, while the growing context steadily inflates the input size of every subsequent call. The total consumption of a task is therefore hard to predict before execution and the prediction must be revised as the run unfolds. In this paper, we propose TokenCast, which learns a composable cost representation for each execution segment, recording its own consumption and the context growth it
case_studies.summary: TokenCast predicts how many tokens an LLM agent will use while it runs, helping you estimate costs even though token use can jump wildly between runs. It builds a lightweight model that learns a cost for each step of the agent’s plan and updates the prediction as the context grows. The result is a more reliable budget for running large‑model agents in production.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM workloads, use TokenCast: 1) integrate its cost‑model API into your orchestration layer; 2) feed the model with recent run data to initialise it; 3) adjust your budget thresholds based on the predicted token totals.
case_studies.score_reasoning: TokenCast offers a practical method to forecast LLM token usage during agent execution, which is directly relevant to managing costs and performance for cloud-based LLM deployments in SaaS environments. The novelty is modest as the core idea builds on existing cost estimation concepts, but the composable cost representation provides a useful tool for IT engineers to anticipate billing and resource allocation. The paper’s approach can be implemented within 90 days by integrating the cost model into existing LLM orchestration pipelines or API usage dashboards. The total exceeds the 40 threshold, so low_signal is set to false.

case_studies.title: MINT: Modeling GenAI Impact on Network Traffic
case_studies.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is becoming a mainstream network workload, yet packet-level simulators lack measure\-ment-driven GenAI traffic models. Currently researchers must approximate GenAI services using traditional sources such as file transfer and video streaming, limiting realistic network evaluation of scheduling and capacity planning. We present MINT, a measurement and modeling framework for GenAI network traffic. Using an isolated net\-work-namespace capture pipeline, we collect client-side traces from three LLM providers across four modalities, cloud and edge servers, and wired and wireles
case_studies.summary: MINT is a toolkit that captures real network traffic from large language model (LLM) services and builds statistical models of that traffic. The authors ran a controlled capture across several cloud and edge servers and four AI modalities, then used those traces to create traffic models that reflect true GenAI workloads rather than generic file‑transfer or video traffic. The result is a set of reproducible models that can be plugged into network simulators or traffic generators.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infra, here is what to do: 1) run MINT’s capture pipeline on your own LLM endpoints to collect real traffic traces; 2) feed those traces into your network simulation or capacity‑planning tool to replace generic traffic models; 3) re‑evaluate scheduling and bandwidth allocation based on the new GenAI traffic patterns.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a new, measurement‑driven framework (MINT) for modeling GenAI network traffic, which is novel relative to existing packet‑level simulators that rely on generic traffic proxies. It is directly relevant to IT engineers managing cloud and edge infrastructure, network capacity planning, and SSO/SSO traffic patterns for LLM APIs, earning a solid IT relevance score. While the methodology can be leveraged to build traffic models or simulate capacity within 90 days, the lack of ready‑to‑deploy tooling and the need for specialized capture pipelines limits immediate actionable use, so the 90‑day value is moderate. Overall, the contribution is sufficiently interesting and applicable to raise the total score above the 40 threshold.

case_studies.title: Tracekit: Tamper-Evident Intent-Reasoning-Action Auditing for Autonomous Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Autonomous coding agents read untrusted files, run shell commands and spawn sub-agents with little supervision, yet their record is usually an editable log. We present Tracekit, an open-source, dependency-free system that captures three channels for every agent session: what the human asked (intent), what the model said of its reasoning (self-report), and what it actually executed (actions). These are written to a hash-chained, externally anchorable ledger and cross-checked. Tracekit hooks into Claude Code's lifecycle events, reconstructs multi-agent hierarchies, gates tool calls with a pre-ex
case_studies.summary: Tracekit records three logs – the user’s intent, the model’s self‑reported reasoning, and the actions actually carried out – and stores them in a hash‑chained ledger that can be anchored externally, preventing tampering. The system hooks into Claude Code’s events to build a hierarchy of agent interactions and gate tool usage with pre‑checks. This gives an auditable, tamper‑evident trail for autonomous coding agents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that runs autonomous coding agents, step 1: integrate Tracekit into the agent lifecycle to capture intent, reasoning, and actions; step 2: configure the hash‑chained ledger to anchor logs to an external, immutable store (e.g., a blockchain or S3 bucket with versioning); step 3: set pre‑checks for tool calls to ensure only authorised commands execute and monitor the ledger for anomalies.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces Tracekit, an audit framework that captures intent, reasoning, and actions of autonomous coding agents, with a hash‑chained ledger for tamper evidence. This is directly useful for IT engineers managing AI‑driven code generation workflows, offering a mechanism to enforce security, compliance, and operational traceability. The system hooks into existing LLM lifecycles, making it actionable within current cloud environments (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) and can be integrated into DevOps pipelines or MLOps platforms. The novelty lies in the combination of intent‑reasoning‑action capture and tamper‑evident storage, a concept rarely addressed in practice. Practical use cases include building automated compliance checks, generating audit reports for client engagements, and detecting malicious agent behavior within 90 days.

case_studies.title: When Valid Tool Calls Change Meaning: Formation-Consistent Dispatch for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Tool-enabled agents form calls from model-visible interfaces, while hosts later select their implementation. Standard dispatch omits the descriptor-handler relation. An unchanged and schema-valid call can therefore acquire a different security effect during rollout, reconnect, or delayed approval. We call this failure schema-epoch drift. We present formation-consistent dispatch (FCD), which connects implementation analysis to execution authority. Reviewed profiles produce provenance-bound over-approximations of declared in-scope effects from official source. Under a closed-target approval poli
case_studies.summary: When an LLM agent calls a tool, the same call can later be executed with a different implementation, creating a security gap known as schema‑epoch drift. The authors propose Formation‑Consistent Dispatch (FCD) to tie the tool’s implementation to its declared effect, providing provenance‑bound safety checks. This approach ensures that any tool call used in cloud‑managed services remains consistent and secure across updates and deployments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑enabled cloud services, adopt FCD by: 1) mapping each tool to its authorised implementation; 2) validating every call against this map before execution; 3) auditing changes to tool definitions for drift risks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a specific security issue—schema‑epoch drift—in tool‑enabled LLM agents, offering a concrete dispatch method (FCD) that could be applied in managed SaaS or cloud environments. It provides actionable insights that IT engineers could use to harden agent deployments, making it of medium novelty, high relevance, and high short‑term value.

case_studies.title: RSI-Router: Evolving Subtask-Level LLM Routing and Skills for Cost-Efficient Agents
case_studies.abstract: Practical deployment of large language model (LLM) agents requires strong task performance at affordable inference cost. For long-horizon agentic tasks, this performance-cost trade-off can be improved through within-task large-small model collaboration, as smaller models can handle some stages even when they cannot solve the full task. In this paper, we introduce RSI-router, a routing framework that constructs subtask-level model assignments and model-specific skills through recursive self-improvement over accumulated experience. Each iteration consists of four stages: Subtask Mining derives s
case_studies.summary: RSI‑Router tackles the high cost of running large language models by automatically assigning subtasks to smaller, cheaper models when they are sufficient, improving overall efficiency without sacrificing performance. It builds a framework that mines subtasks, creates model‑specific skills, and recursively improves routing decisions based on experience. The result is a more cost‑effective agent that still meets complex task requirements.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) Identify long‑horizon tasks your services run; 2) Deploy RSI‑Router to split these tasks into subtasks and assign smaller models to appropriate steps; 3) Monitor inference cost and performance, iterating on routing rules to keep costs low while maintaining quality.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a routing framework that dynamically assigns sub‑tasks to appropriately sized LLMs to reduce inference cost while maintaining performance. 1) Novelty: 26 – the idea of recursive self‑improvement for sub‑task routing and skill construction is a fresh take that an IT engineer might find intriguing. 2) IT relevance: 29 – the approach directly concerns LLM API usage, cost optimisation, and agent‑based automation, all of which are central to modern IT infrastructure. 3) Value in 90 days: 31 – the concepts can be prototyped with existing LLM services, enabling engineers to build cost‑aware agents, automate routine queries, or integrate routing logic into existing workflows. 4) Total score: 86 (well above 40), so "low_signal" is false.

case_studies.title: AgentWare: Automating the Lifecycle of Agentic Applications across the Edge-to-Cloud Continuum
case_studies.abstract: Deploying LLM-enabled agentic applications across the Edge-to-Cloud continuum remains challenging due to hardware heterogeneity, deployment complexity, limited observability, and the lack of systematic evaluation methods. Existing solutions address agent development, observability, or benchmarking separately, offering limited support for the full lifecycle of distributed agentic applications. This paper presents AgentWare, an AgenticOps framework that automates the provisioning, deployment, observability, and evaluation of agentic applications across Edge-to-Cloud infrastructures. AgentWare in
case_studies.summary: AgentWare automates provisioning, deployment, observability, and evaluation of LLM‑enabled agentic apps across edge and cloud, solving the problem of scattered tools and manual work. It built a unified AgenticOps framework that manages hardware heterogeneity, simplifies deployment, adds telemetry, and provides benchmarking. The result is faster, more reliable roll‑outs of complex distributed agent applications.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) integrate AgentWare’s deployment engine with your existing CI/CD pipelines; 2) use its observability hooks to collect telemetry from edge and cloud nodes; 3) run the built‑in evaluation suite to benchmark agent performance and adjust resource allocation.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a comprehensive framework (AgentWare) that automates provisioning, deployment, observability, and evaluation of agentic applications across edge-to-cloud infrastructures, directly impacting IT engineers’ workflow in cloud, DevOps, and security contexts. The novelty lies in integrating these lifecycle stages into a single tool, which is surprising and useful for engineers managing heterogeneous environments. The practical value is high: engineers could adopt or adapt the framework to streamline their own agent deployment pipelines, implement observability, and benchmark performance within 90 days.
